notes.b: Before a performer can improve, they need to know exactly where they stand. Performance analysis is the systematic observation, measurement and evaluation of a performance, or part of it, to identify strengths and weaknesses and inform improvement.
points: Systematic means the same observation or measurement method is used each time, so results can be compared fairly, rather than relying on a general impression of how the performance went.
It can cover a whole performance, such as a full match or routine, or one part of it, such as one phase of a jump or one set play (a rehearsed team move).
Strengths are identified so they can be kept, and weaknesses are identified so they can be targeted in training, which stops time being wasted on things already done well.
Analysis is used at the start of a plan to find priorities and again at the end to measure progress, so the same method gives a fair before-and-after comparison.
notes.tip: If asked to explain performance analysis, give the definition (systematic observation, measurement and evaluation) and say it identifies strengths and weaknesses to inform improvement. Name methods only in general terms here.

notes.b: Analysis replaces guesswork with evidence before the performer decides what to train. This is why athletes carry out a performance analysis, and each benefit below is a reason you can use.
points: Objective evidence: recorded data, such as counts of successful actions or measured times, replaces opinion about how well the performance went, so the performer is not misled by feelings.
Identifies priorities: it shows which weaknesses cost the most performance, so training time goes to them first.
Sets realistic goals: current levels are measured, so goals can be set just beyond them rather than at an unknown level.
Tracks progress: repeated analysis shows whether training is working and when a target has been reached.
Motivates: measurable improvement shows the performer that effort is producing results, which encourages them to keep training.
Improves decision-making: evidence of which choices succeeded in a performance helps the performer choose better in future.
Improves technique: analysis pinpoints which part of a movement needs changing, so practice is aimed at the actual fault.
notes.tip: Questions ask for two benefits or why athletes would analyse performance. Pick two, and for each say what the evidence lets the performer do, for example priorities are identified so training targets the biggest weakness.

notes.b: Performance analysis is the first of four linked stages. Each stage feeds the next, and the results of the final stage start the next cycle. The next three subsections cover stages 2 to 4 in detail.
points: Stage 1, analyse: observe and measure the performance and identify strengths and weaknesses.
Stage 2, set goals: turn the weaknesses into realistic performance goals based on sound theory (principles known to work in training).
Stage 3, train or practise: carry out a designed programme, monitor it with ongoing evidence, reflect on it and adapt it where needed.
Stage 4, concluding analysis: evaluate a performance using the same methods as the first analysis, so the two can be compared fairly.
The results of the concluding analysis inform the next set of goals, which is why it is a cycle and not a straight line.

notes.b: Physical factors set what a performer's body can do. They decide how hard and how long someone can train and perform, so a weakness here limits everything else.
points: Fitness levels: the health-related and performance-related components of fitness set how long and how hard a performer can work; a sprinter depends on speed and power, while a long-distance swimmer depends on endurance.
Health: illness reduces training time and the energy available for practice, lowering performance until the performer recovers.
Injury: an injury stops or limits training and can change movement patterns, so technique and fitness both suffer until rehabilitation (the recovery programme) is complete.
Body type: height, limb length and body mass affect suitability for an activity; a tall basketball player has an advantage in rebounding.
Age and maturation (physical development): physical maturity affects strength, speed and size, so the same training load can suit one young performer and overload another.
Fatigue: tired muscles lose strength and co-ordination, so late in a match a player's shooting accuracy and decision-making decline.

notes.b: Technical factors are about how well a skill is carried out. Two performers with the same fitness can perform very differently if one has better technique.
points: Level of skill: a performer who has learned the correct technique for a skill, such as a golf putt, repeats it more often under pressure.
Technique: efficient technique uses less energy for the same output, so a sprinter with an efficient running action produces more speed from the same effort.
Consistency: a performer who repeats the same technique under different conditions produces more reliable results, because the movement does not break down when circumstances change.

notes.b: Tactical factors are about thinking and reading the game; psychological factors are about the performer's mind. Both decide whether physical ability and skill are used well on the day.
points: Game understanding: recognising patterns of play, such as an attacking team leaving space behind its defence, lets a performer anticipate and move before the play develops.
Decision-making: choosing between passing, shooting and dribbling in the time available; poor choices waste possession even when skill is high.
Knowledge of structures and strategies: knowing a team's set plays and the opponent's defensive system lets a player fit into the plan.
Confidence: a confident performer attempts difficult actions, such as a long-range shot in football, that a doubtful performer avoids.

Anxiety and arousal (how alert and excited the body and mind are): too much arousal causes tension and poor co-ordination, while too little leaves the performer sluggish; the best level differs between performers and tasks.
Motivation: a performer who wants to improve practises more and persists with difficult drills, so training gains are larger.
Concentration: a performer who loses focus during a game misses cues, such as a team-mate's run or a change in the opponent's position.
notes.tip: Don't redefine fitness components or psychological terms at length. Name the factor, then say how it changes performance with a short example from a sport.

notes.b: What a performer does away from training, and the people around them, can help or hold back performance as much as the training itself.
points: Diet and hydration: a balanced diet supplies energy for training and recovery, and dehydration reduces endurance and concentration.
Sleep: sleep allows the body to recover from training, so a performer short of sleep recovers more slowly and performs below their level.
Alcohol and smoking: smoking reduces lung capacity and oxygen delivery, and alcohol impairs recovery and co-ordination.
Balancing study, work and training: time pressure can cut training volume or sleep, so the performer must plan rest and practice around other commitments.
Family support: encouragement, transport to training and financial help allow a young performer to attend sessions; without them participation may be limited.
Peers and team-mates: a supportive group raises effort and enjoyment, while a poor team environment lowers motivation and confidence.
Coach relationship: a coach who gives clear feedback and earns trust helps a performer improve, while a poor relationship makes instructions harder to act on.
Role models: a performer may copy the technique or dedication of an admired athlete, which can raise standards or set unrealistic expectations.

notes.b: The conditions and facilities around a performance can change what the performer is able to do, even when their fitness and skill stay the same.
points: Weather: wind alters the flight of a ball or an arrow, and rain makes surfaces slippery.
Playing surface: a wet or uneven pitch changes the bounce of a ball and the footing of a player.
Quality of facilities and equipment: well-fitted equipment supports correct technique, while worn or badly fitted equipment causes errors or injury.
Access to coaching: a performer far from a qualified coach has fewer structured sessions and less feedback.
Home or away venue: a home venue brings familiar surfaces and crowd support, while an away venue brings travel fatigue and unfamiliar conditions.
Altitude: thinner air at height gives less oxygen per breath, reducing endurance performance until the body acclimatises (adjusts to the conditions).
Heat: high temperatures increase fatigue and sweat loss and raise the risk of heat illness, so performance drops in long events.

notes.b: Sport costs money, and money decides which equipment, clubs and coaching a performer can use. This is why two equally talented performers may not get equal opportunities.
points: Cost of equipment: specialist equipment, such as a bicycle or skis, may be unaffordable, limiting participation and access to the best kit.
Membership fees: club and gym membership fees limit how often a performer can train and which facilities they can use.
Travel costs: travel to training, competitions and coaching can make participation expensive, especially for performers far from clubs.
Coaching fees: private coaching can improve technique quickly but may be out of reach for many performers.

notes.h: Choosing the two most important factors
notes.b: Exam questions often name an activity and ask for the two factors that matter most. The method is to pick the two that most affect performance in that activity, preferably from different groups, and link each to specific moments of performance.
points: Start by listing what the activity demands; the factors that match those demands are the most important.
Basketball free-throw shooter: technique and concentration are the two most important factors, because the shot is a repeated movement taken alone under pressure.
Technique: a small fault in the release shows in every attempt, so technique largely determines accuracy.
Concentration: the shooter must block out the crowd and the score and complete the same routine before each shot, so concentration decides whether the routine is completed.
Marathon runner: cardio-respiratory endurance (the ability of the heart and lungs to supply oxygen over a long time) and pacing/motivation are the two most important factors.
Endurance decides whether pace holds after the halfway point; pacing and motivation decide whether the runner keeps pushing through the final stages when fatigue rises.
notes.tip: The question asks you to identify two factors and discuss why. Name both, then justify each with a link to the activity, such as a specific moment in the free throw or the final stages of a marathon, not just a definition.

keyTerms.definition: The systematic observation, measurement and evaluation of a performance, or part of it, to identify strengths and weaknesses and inform improvement.
The four linked stages of analysing performance, setting goals, training with monitoring and reflection, and concluding analysis.
An evaluation of performance at the end of a programme, using the same methods as the initial analysis.
Recognising patterns of play and anticipating what is likely to happen next.
Choosing an action, such as a pass, shot or dribble, in the time available.
The ability to repeat the same technique or result under varying conditions.
Physical development towards adult size, strength and body function.
Distributing effort across an event so that energy is not spent too early.
The body's gradual adaptation to altitude or heat over days or weeks.

questions.prompt: Identify and discuss the two most important factors that influence performance in a physical activity of your choice.
questions.model: Activity: basketball free-throw shooting. Factor 1, technique (technical group): the shot is the same repeated movement each time, so a consistent release point and a stable, balanced set-up decide whether the ball goes in. A player whose elbow flares out or whose feet are not set will miss in a predictable pattern, and the fault appears under pressure, when the shot matters most. Factor 2, concentration (psychological group): the shot is taken alone after a pause, with the crowd and the score as distractions. A shooter who loses focus during the pre-shot routine rushes the release, so a technically sound shot is missed. The two factors come from different groups, so the physical skill and the mental state both decide the outcome of the shot.

questions.prompt: Explain performance analysis and describe two benefits of it for a performer.
questions.model: Performance analysis is the systematic observation, measurement and evaluation of a performance, or part of it, to identify strengths and weaknesses and inform improvement. Benefit 1: it provides objective evidence, so the performer and coach act on recorded data rather than impression, for example by knowing exactly how many shots in training succeeded. Benefit 2: it identifies priorities and supports realistic goals, because the weakest measured area is targeted first and goals are set from the performer's current level.
